thread.previously: The war began in late February. In late October Iran claimed strikes on tankers in Hormuz, and Brent rose above $110. On 31 October Trump said one or two Iranian sites, including Pickaxe Mountain, remained to be hit. Khamenei ordered an unrestricted response to any threat. Iranian negotiators in Qatar are discussing a two-day plan: US measures on day one, Hormuz reopened on day two. The US has not publicly replied. Brent fell about 3% on 2 November.
thread.changed: New: AP reports Netanyahu pressed Trump to strike Iran after the 3 November midterms. Iran spelled out its two-day plan's conditions. Houthis claimed drones toward Dammam. Reports say Gulf allies were told to prepare from 4 November.

stories.headline: Iran offers two-day deal as Netanyahu reportedly urges post-midterm strikes
stories.question: Is the US-Iran war heading for a quick deal, or a bigger attack after the midterms?
stories.dek: Both paths are still open. Iran has squeezed its ceasefire plan into two days. A report says Netanyahu urged Trump to strike after 3 November. Oil prices are tracking the odds.

so_far.text: The war began on 28 February 2026, when the US and Israel struck Iran. Since then the US has blockaded Iran's ports, and Iran claims control of the Strait of Hormuz, the sea lane out of the Gulf. Ships nearby have been hit. On 30 October Qatar's gas tanker Al Mayeda was struck by 'unidentified objects'. On 31 October Trump spoke with Netanyahu and afterwards called the call productive. Qatar and Pakistan carry messages between the US and Iran, because there are no direct talks.

what_happened.text: On 2 November Iran said its seven-step ceasefire plan is unchanged but has been condensed to run in two days, not seven. Its conditions: the US lifts its naval blockade, repeals sanctions, guarantees an end to strikes and agrees a full regional ceasefire, especially in Lebanon. Hormuz would then reopen and nuclear talks would resume. Spokesman Esmaeil Baghaei gave no sign that Washington had agreed. Also on 2 November, AP cited unnamed officials who said Netanyahu pressed Trump to attack Iran after the 3 November midterms. The pressure came during a weekend call, the officials said. Netanyahu has not commented. The Houthis said they launched drones toward Saudi Arabia's Dammam airport.

steps.text: Each side holds a lever. The US has its blockade of Iran's ports, and Iran has its grip on Hormuz.
Neither side wants to let go first, so Iran's plan asks the US to meet conditions before Hormuz reopens.
Squeezing seven steps into two days shortens the gap in which either side could back out.
Trump reportedly wants to give talks more time and decide after the 3 November midterms, which makes that date a decision point.
If talks stall, strikes could follow. Reports say the US told Gulf allies to prepare from as early as 4 November.

lesson.concept: How oil prices put a price on war risk
lesson.big_idea: An oil price is partly a bet on the future. When war could cut supply, traders blend the calm price and the crisis price, weighted by how likely each seems.

steps.title: Price is a bet on supply
steps.text: Oil is bought for delivery weeks ahead. So the current price depends on how much oil traders expect to flow soon, not only on what is flowing right now.

steps.title: Picture two possible futures
steps.text: In this war, picture two outcomes. A deal reopens Hormuz, more tankers sail and oil gets cheaper. New strikes mean more ships hit near Hormuz and less oil, so oil gets dearer.

steps.title: Blend them by the odds
steps.text: Traders roughly blend the two prices by how likely each seems. Multiply each price by its chance, then add the results. Economists call this an 'expected value'.

steps.title: News moves odds, odds move price
steps.text: The extra paid above the calm price is the 'risk premium'. A report that makes a deal look likelier shrinks it. On 2 November Brent fell over 3% after one such report.

example.setup: Imagine traders think oil would be worth $90 a barrel if a deal reopens Hormuz, and $130 if the war widens. Assume they see each outcome as equally likely.

lines.label: Deal share
lines.note: Calm price weighted by its odds

lines.label: War share
lines.note: Crisis price weighted by its odds

lines.label: Blended price
lines.note: What a barrel trades at

lines.label: Deal odds rise
lines.note: A report makes talks look likelier

lines.label: New price
lines.note: Down $4, or about 3.6%

example.result: Nothing physical changed, and no extra tanker sailed. The odds moved by ten points, and the price fell $4. That is why reports alone can swing oil.

apply.text: On 2 November Brent fell over 3%, to just under $110, after a report that Trump wants to give diplomacy more time. No deal was signed; only the odds moved. Rabobank's Florence Schmit called it 'a temporary pullback'. AP reports Netanyahu urged strikes after the midterms. If such strikes look likelier, the odds and the price could swing back up.

practice.q: Same two prices, $90 and $130. Suppose reports of strikes from 4 November push the odds of war to 70%. What is the new price?
practice.answer: Deal share: 30% × $90 = $27. War share: 70% × $130 = $91. Add them: $27 + $91 = $118. The price rises $8 from $110, even though nothing has changed at sea yet.

check.why: No deal was signed and Hormuz did not reopen. A report that Trump wants more time for talks changed the odds, and the price followed.

takeaways: Oil prices blend a calm price and a crisis price, weighted by the odds of each.

thread.previously: US midterms on 3 November 2026 decide 435 House seats, 35 Senate seats and 36 governorships. Trump ended a 28-stop campaign on 1 November in Iowa and Kansas. A Harvard tool gives Democrats 96% (House) and 76% (Senate) odds. An NBC poll has 52–45 for a Democratic Congress. A judge dismissed the Justice Department's Alaska suit. Polls close 4:30–11:30 a.m. IST on 4 November.
thread.changed: New: Trump says he will be "Mr Veto" if Republicans lose. Guides warn the House majority may not be confirmed until mid-November, and Senate control could slip to January 2027.

stories.headline: US votes for Congress, but full results may take weeks
stories.question: What is at stake in the US midterms, and when will we know who won?
stories.dek: Americans choose all 435 House seats and 35 Senate seats on 3 November. The result shapes whether Trump can pass laws or turns to vetoes. Some results could take until mid-November or January 2027.

so_far.text: The midterms are US national elections held halfway through a president's four-year term. They choose Congress, the body that writes US laws. Congress has two chambers: the House of Representatives and the Senate. On 3 November 2026, Americans vote for all 435 House seats and 35 Senate seats. Democrats are favoured to win the House. The Senate race is closer. President Donald Trump is not on the ballot, but the result decides how much he can get done.

what_happened.text: In remarks reported on 2 November, Trump said he would become "Mr Veto" if Republicans lose the midterms. Voting takes place on 3 November. The first polls close at 6 p.m. Eastern Time (ET) in Indiana and Kentucky, which is 4:30 a.m. IST on 4 November. California closes at 11 p.m. ET (9:30 a.m. IST). Alaska closes last, at 1 a.m. ET (11:30 a.m. IST). Californians also vote on Proposition 40, a one-time 5% tax on billionaires, mostly to pay for health care. Wealthy opponents are spending heavily against it.

steps.text: Congress passes bills, and the president either signs them into law or vetoes them, which means rejecting them.
Democrats are favoured to win the House, and holding one chamber lets a party block bills, though not pass laws alone.
Trump's "Mr Veto" pledge signals he would reject bills he dislikes, so few new laws would pass.
Overturning a veto needs two-thirds of both chambers, a level a narrow majority rarely reaches.
Control itself may also wait, because slow mail counts and possible runoffs can delay the final seat totals.

lesson.concept: How a race is called before every vote is counted
lesson.big_idea: A race is "called" when the trailing candidate cannot realistically catch up with the ballots still left. If too many ballots remain, or the gap is tiny, everyone has to wait.

steps.title: Votes are counted in batches
steps.text: Ballots cast on Election Day, early votes and mail ballots are often counted at different speeds. One guide says California counts mail ballots slowly, which could delay confirming the House majority until mid-November.

steps.title: Compare the gap with what's left
steps.text: At any moment a race has a gap, meaning the leader's lead, and a pile of uncounted ballots. If the pile is smaller than the gap, the result cannot change.

steps.title: Work out the share needed
steps.text: If the pile is bigger, ask how many votes the trailer needs to tie: (ballots left + gap) ÷ 2. Divide that by the ballots left. The higher that share, the safer the call.

steps.title: Too close means wait
steps.text: When the needed share is realistic, nobody calls the race. Very close races can need a recount. Some, as in Georgia, can go to a runoff, a second vote that could push results to January 2027.

steps.title: Add up seats for control
steps.text: Control of a chamber needs a majority, meaning more than half its seats. All 435 House seats are being contested. So the House is decided only when one party's called seats pass the halfway mark.

example.setup: Say a House race has counted most votes. Candidate A has 52,000 and Candidate B has 48,000. Assume 20,000 mail ballots are still uncounted.

lines.label: The gap
lines.note: A's lead right now.

lines.label: Pile left
lines.note: So B could still catch up, in theory.

lines.label: Votes B needs to tie
lines.note: B must beat A by 4,000 within the pile.

lines.label: Share B needs
lines.note: B must win 60% of remaining ballots.

lines.label: Check the tie
lines.note: B's 4,000 edge exactly cancels A's lead.

lines.label: The call
lines.calc: Mail splitting about 50–50 means A wins
lines.note: If mail leans heavily to B, callers wait.

example.result: B needs 60% of the remaining ballots just to tie. If mail ballots have been splitting evenly, A can be called the winner. If they lean strongly to B, the race stays open.

apply.text: This is why control may not be clear on 4 November, even after the last polls close at 11:30 a.m. IST. California counts mail ballots slowly, so close races there can stay uncalled. One guide says the House majority may not be confirmed until mid-November. In the Senate, a Georgia runoff could push control to January 2027.

practice.q: Candidate A leads by 3,000 votes with 10,000 ballots left. What share of those ballots must Candidate B win to tie?
practice.answer: Votes B needs: (10,000 + 3,000) ÷ 2 = 6,500. Share: 6,500 ÷ 10,000 = 65%. Check: A gets 3,500, and 6,500 − 3,500 = 3,000, which cancels the lead. B needs 65%, so a call is likely unless the ballots lean heavily to B.

check.q: A candidate leads by 2,000 votes and only 1,500 ballots are left. Can the race be called?
options: No, every race must wait for a full count

Only if the remaining ballots are mail ballots
check.why: The trailer can gain at most 1,500 votes. That is less than the 2,000-vote gap, so the result cannot change.

takeaways: A race is called when the trailer cannot catch up with the ballots still left.
Control of Congress decides whether Trump passes laws or, as he says, becomes 'Mr Veto'.

scenes.say: Why does it matter? Congress writes the bills. The president signs them or vetoes them. Trump says if Republicans lose, he will become Mr Veto.
In India, results arrive on the morning of the fourth of November. The first polls close at four thirty, Indian time. Alaska closes last, at eleven thirty.

But closed polls do not mean a winner. A race is called only when the trailer cannot catch up. Say candidate A leads by four thousand votes, with twenty thousand ballots left. To tie, candidate B needs twelve thousand of them. That is sixty per cent.

Remember: a race is called when the gap cannot be closed. Watch from four thirty in the morning, Indian time, on the fourth of November.

stories.headline: Two Kuki youths found dead, and protests erupt in Manipur's Kangpokpi
stories.question: Why has violence flared again in Manipur after two missing Kuki men were found dead?
stories.dek: Two Kuki youths went missing on 29 October and were found dead on 1 November. No one has been arrested, Kuki-Naga mistrust is rising, and protests in Kangpokpi turned into clashes with police.

so_far.text: Manipur, a state in India's north-east, is home to several communities, including Meitei, Kuki and Naga people. In May 2023, a conflict broke out between Meiteis and Kukis. Manipur was later placed under President's rule, which means the central government runs the state directly. That ended on 4 February 2026, when an elected government returned. Yumnam Khemchand Singh became Chief Minister. His two deputies come from different communities: Nemcha Kipgen, a Kuki-Zo leader from the BJP, and Losii Dikho, a Naga leader from the NPF.

what_happened.text: T Chongloi, 21, and Paoginlal Hangsing, 20, went missing from Taphou Kuki village on 29 October. Some reports say 28 October. On 1 November, their bodies were found in gunny bags at a banana farm in a hilly part of Senapati district. Reports say the bodies were mutilated. No cause of death or suspect has been named. That night, protests spread across Kangpokpi district. Protesters burned tyres, blocked roads with logs and boulders, and threw stones. Police used tear gas and baton charges. Hindustan Times reported three people injured. On 2 November, more security forces were sent in, and some roads were cleared.

steps.text: Manipur has been split along ethnic lines since May 2023, so people quickly read any killing as one community attacking another.
On 31 October, three Kuki men died in a gunfight in Noney district. Kuki groups blamed Naga militants, and NSCN-IM denied involvement.
Then the two youths were found dead in Senapati. These were more Kuki deaths within days, though reports name no suspects.
No one has been arrested. So protesters block roads and refuse to take the bodies home, to put pressure on the government.
The anger has reached the cabinet. A Kuki body wants the Naga Deputy CM to resign, which tests the government's power-sharing between communities.

lesson.concept: How police jurisdiction decides who investigates a crime
lesson.big_idea: In India, every place comes under one police station and one district police chief. That chief's team investigates crimes there.

steps.title: Police belong to the state
steps.text: Policing is a state subject under India's Constitution, so each state runs its own police. A Superintendent of Police, or SP, heads each district's police.

steps.title: Every spot has one station
steps.text: Each district has several police stations, each covering an area. A crime is recorded at the station covering where it happened. That record is an FIR, or first information report.

steps.title: That station builds the case
steps.text: Its officers order a post-mortem, the medical exam that finds the cause of death. They gather evidence, question witnesses and make arrests.

steps.title: Areas and cases can move
steps.text: The state can move a village to another district's police, or hand a case to a special team. Governments often do this when people distrust local police.

steps.title: Trust is the hidden ingredient
steps.text: Where ethnic conflict divides people, they may doubt police they see as close to another community. In Kangpokpi, a protest committee wants Taphou Kuki village placed under the Kangpokpi SP.

example.setup: Imagine a village called Hillside near the border of District A and District B. Two of its young men are found dead in District A.

lines.label: Stage 1: the report
lines.calc: FIR filed at a District A station
lines.note: The bodies were found there.

lines.label: Stage 2: the probe
lines.note: Post-mortem, evidence and arrests.

lines.label: Stage 3: doubt
lines.calc: Hillside families distrust District A police
lines.note: They fear evidence may be mishandled.

lines.label: Stage 4: pressure
lines.calc: Roadblocks; bodies kept back until arrests
lines.note: Protest pushes the government to act.

lines.label: Stage 5: the options
lines.calc: Move Hillside to District B, or appoint special team
lines.note: Either choice changes who holds the case.

example.result: After a killing, an early fight is often over who investigates. If people distrust the investigator, even a correct finding may not calm them.

apply.text: In this case, the bodies were found in Senapati district. The Committee on Tribal Unity wants Taphou Kuki village under the Kangpokpi SP. It says the bodies will not be taken to the village until arrests are made. Separately, the Naga Peoples' Organisation has demanded an impartial probe and warned against tampering with evidence.

practice.q: Suppose someone is robbed in District B but reports it at a station in District A, where they live. Who investigates?
practice.answer: Step 1: the crime happened in District B. Step 2: the District A station still records it as a 'zero FIR', an FIR filed outside the correct area. Step 3: it sends the FIR to District B. Step 4: District B's officers investigate.

terms.meaning: The officer who heads the police in one district.
When the central government runs a state directly, with no elected state government.
First information report: the police record that formally starts a criminal case.
An investigation run by people who favour neither side.

check.q: Why would a community care which district's police chief covers its village?
options: That chief's officers lead the investigation, gather evidence and make arrests.
That chief decides the punishment for anyone found guilty.
That chief controls the state's elected government.
check.why: Police build the case by collecting evidence and making arrests. Courts decide punishment. So if people distrust the investigator, they doubt the whole case.

takeaways: The police area where a crime happens decides who investigates, so trust in those police matters.
Two Kuki youths were found dead on 1 November, and Kangpokpi protests turned into clashes with police.
Watch for arrests, the cause of death, and any change in which police chief covers the village.

stories.headline: Airfares are rising, and the Supreme Court won't rush to intervene
stories.question: Why are Indian airfares soaring, and will anyone stop them rising further?
stories.dek: IndiGo's chief says record fuel costs may push fares higher. The Supreme Court won't hear a fare plea urgently, and the Centre says rules to curb fare swings are being fast-tracked.

so_far.text: Last year, social activist S Laxminarayanan filed a petition in the Supreme Court. He claims airlines charge high fares around festival seasons. In January 2026 the Supreme Court raised concern over these festival-season fare rises. Then airline costs climbed. IndiGo cited higher prices for ATF (aviation turbine fuel, the jet fuel planes burn) during the US-Iran war. It raised its fuel charge on all flights from 6 October 2026. Indian airlines also suspended flights to Saudi Arabia. Air India set its cancellations until 20 October, and Akasa Air paused Riyadh flights until 24 October.

what_happened.text: On 2 November 2026 the Supreme Court refused urgent listing, meaning an early hearing, for the plea. The plea alleges a 700% hike in airfares. The court remarked: "Don't travel by air." The Centre told the court it is fast-tracking rules under the Bharatiya Vayuyan Adhiniyam, India's aviation law. It said the rules aim to curb fare swings and protect passengers. The same day, NDTV reported IndiGo chief executive Willie Walsh saying fares may rise as fuel costs hit record highs. Air India, Akasa Air and IndiGo extended their Saudi Arabia cancellations again.

steps.text: Jet fuel is one of an airline's biggest costs, so when fuel prices jump, every flight costs more to run.
Airlines pass that cost on through a fuel charge added to tickets, as IndiGo did from 6 October 2026.
Fares also climb as cheaper seats sell out, so festival rush days bring the steepest prices.
The Centre says new rules will curb fare swings, but it is not yet known whether they will cap fares.

for_you.text: If you plan to fly soon, especially around festivals, expect high fares. IndiGo's higher fuel charge applies to all its flights from 6 October 2026. If you are booked to Saudi Arabia on Air India, Akasa Air or IndiGo, check your flight, because cancellations were extended. Booking early usually helps, since cheaper seats sell first. lesson.concept: How airline fares climb as seats fill up
lesson.big_idea: An airline doesn't sell every seat at one price. It sells seats in price groups, cheapest first. As seats fill, fares step up, and rising costs like fuel lift every step.

steps.title: Seats sold in price groups
steps.text: Airlines split a flight's seats into groups called fare buckets. Each bucket has its own price. The cheapest bucket is offered first, and it holds only some of the seats.

steps.title: Sold-out buckets push prices up
steps.text: When one bucket sells out, the booking system opens the next, dearer bucket. So the same seat on the same flight can cost far more a week later.

steps.title: Costs lift every bucket
steps.text: A fuel charge sits on top of the base fare. When fuel costs rise, the charge rises and every bucket gets dearer. IndiGo raised its fuel charge from 6 October 2026.

steps.title: Reading percentage rises correctly
steps.text: A percentage rise is the increase divided by the starting price. A 100% rise doubles a fare. The 700% hike the plea alleges would mean paying eight times the original fare.

example.setup: Imagine a 100-seat flight in festival week. Assume three fare buckets: 40 seats at ₹4,000, 40 at ₹8,000 and 20 at ₹16,000. Assume a ₹1,000 fuel charge on every ticket.

lines.label: Early booker pays
lines.note: Cheapest bucket, plus the fuel charge.

lines.label: From seat 41
lines.note: First bucket sold out, so the next one opens.

lines.label: Last 20 seats
lines.note: Late festival bookers land here.

lines.label: Extra paid
lines.note: Same flight, same kind of seat.

lines.label: As a percentage
lines.note: Divide the increase by the starting fare.

lines.label: Fuel charge doubles
lines.note: Higher costs lift even the cheapest bucket.

example.result: No rule is broken, yet the last seat costs more than three times the first. Higher fuel costs then raise even the cheapest seat. Demand and costs push fares up together.

practice.q: A fare rises from ₹3,000 to ₹24,000. What percentage rise is that? Does it match the 700% the plea alleges?
practice.answer: Increase: ₹24,000 − ₹3,000 = ₹21,000. Divide by the starting fare: ₹21,000 ÷ ₹3,000 = 7. That is a 700% rise. So a 700% hike means paying eight times the original fare.

check.why: Airlines sell seats in price groups, cheapest first. Rush days empty the cheap groups early, so late buyers pay the top prices.

takeaways: Fares climb as cheaper seat groups sell out, and fuel costs lift every seat's price.

thread.previously: Investors are testing the AI spending boom. Meta raised AI capex guidance and fell 7%; Alphabet fell about 12% on a profit miss despite strong cloud growth; Intel fell over 28% on a weak outlook. The Nasdaq fell 1.4% on 29 October and nearly 3% on 30 October, ending October down 5.3%. On 1 November the WSJ reported AI investors are hedging against a downturn, and lenders are demanding tougher terms to fund data centres.
thread.changed: New on 2 November: Anthropic's amended IPO filing put hard numbers on the AI spending debate. It shows $895 billion of computing commitments against about $132 billion cash, including $161.2 billion of Broadcom leases.

stories.headline: Anthropic's IPO filing reveals $895 billion in computing promises
stories.question: How can Anthropic promise $895 billion for computing with about $132 billion in cash?
stories.dek: Anthropic has promised about $895 billion for computing, roughly seven times its cash. Its cash covers the next year's bills. After that, the bet works only if revenue keeps growing faster than the bills.

so_far.text: Anthropic, the company that makes the Claude AI assistant, is preparing to sell shares to the public on the Nasdaq. First it must file an S-1, a public document that sets out its finances and risks. The filing arrives in a nervous market. In October, Meta, Alphabet and Intel shares fell on worries about AI spending and profits. The Nasdaq fell about 3% on 30 October and ended the month down 5.3%. Earlier, in February 2026, rival OpenAI told investors it had cut its computing spending target to 2030 to about $600 billion. That was down from the $1.4 trillion figure Altman had touted.

what_happened.text: On 2 November Anthropic filed an amended S-1. It discloses five-year equipment leases with Broadcom and financing entities worth about $161.2 billion in rent, not counting interest. Its total computing and data-centre commitments come to about $895 billion. That is roughly seven times its cash of about $132 billion at end-September. About $70 billion falls due within a year, and nearly $450 billion by end-2030. Revenue for the July–September quarter was about $17 billion, up 47% from $11.6 billion. But Anthropic made a $567 million operating loss, after its first-ever operating profit of $974 million in the quarter before.

steps.text: Training and running AI models needs huge numbers of chips and data centres, booked years ahead.
So Anthropic signs long leases and purchase deals, locking in future payments before the revenue to pay them exists.
Those payments are fixed, but revenue depends on customers, and quarterly growth slowed from 144% to 47%.
Broadcom reportedly also lends Anthropic money, so supplier and lender are tied to the same bet.
The filing warns that if suppliers' own financing tightens, contracted computing could be delayed, repriced, reduced or not delivered.

Warns that tighter financing for its computing suppliers could delay, reprice, reduce or cancel contracted computing, and that defaults could make much of the lease obligations due at once.

for_you.text: This filing has no direct effect on prices, EMIs or jobs in India. It matters more if you hold US technology or Nasdaq-linked funds: the Nasdaq fell 5.3% in October on AI spending worries. And AI tools like Claude run on exactly this rented computing.

lesson.concept: How spending promises are tested against cash and revenue
lesson.big_idea: A company that signs long contracts promises fixed payments for years. The test is simple: can cash in the bank pay the near bills, and can growing revenue pay the later ones?

steps.title: A commitment is a future bill
steps.text: When a company signs a multi-year lease or purchase deal, it promises payments it must make even if business slows. Anthropic's leases with Broadcom and financing entities alone total about $161.2 billion over five years.

steps.title: Sort bills by when they're due
steps.text: Not all bills arrive at once. Of Anthropic's roughly $895 billion in commitments, about $70 billion falls due within a year and nearly $450 billion by end-2030.

steps.title: Near bills against cash
steps.text: Compare the bills due soon with cash in the bank. Anthropic had about $132 billion at end-September, enough to cover the roughly $70 billion due in the next year.

steps.title: Later bills against revenue
steps.text: Cash gets used up, so later bills must be paid from revenue, the money customers pay. Anthropic's quarterly revenue rose 47% to about $17 billion, but growth slowed from 144%.

steps.title: Count only real cash losses
steps.text: Some losses are accounting re-pricings, not spending. Of a $80.7 billion first-half net loss, $72.4 billion was non-cash. The third-quarter operating loss, closer to real running costs, was $567 million.

example.setup: Imagine a cloud-kitchen startup in Pune with ₹100 crore in the bank. It signs five-year equipment leases worth ₹700 crore. ₹50 crore is due in year one. Assume revenue of ₹40 crore a year and no other costs.

lines.label: Promises vs cash
lines.note: The same ratio as in Anthropic's filing.

lines.label: Year one bills
lines.note: Cash covers the near bills comfortably.

lines.label: Left after year one
lines.note: A cushion, but a small one.

lines.label: Years two to five
lines.note: The later bills are much bigger.

lines.label: Revenue needed
lines.note: Revenue must roughly quadruple, and fast.

example.result: The startup is safe this year because its cash covers the near bills. Whether it survives later depends on revenue growing about four times. That is the same kind of bet Anthropic's filing describes.

apply.text: Anthropic is that startup at a far bigger scale. Its about $132 billion cash covers the roughly $70 billion due within a year. But nearly $450 billion falls due by end-2030, far more than its cash. Quarterly revenue is about $17 billion, so it must keep growing fast, even as growth slowed from 144% to 47%.

practice.q: Same startup, but revenue jumps to ₹80 crore a year from year two. Over years two to five, how much of the ₹650 crore is still uncovered?
practice.answer: Revenue over four years: ₹80 crore × 4 = ₹320 crore. Bills: ₹650 crore. Gap: ₹650 − ₹320 = ₹330 crore. Use the ₹90 crore left from year one: ₹330 − ₹90 = ₹240 crore. That still has to come from new loans or faster growth.

A long contract to rent equipment, here chips and servers, for fixed payments.

check.q: Anthropic has about $132 billion cash and about $70 billion due within a year. What is the bigger long-run question?
options: Whether it can pay the next twelve months of bills from cash
Whether revenue grows fast enough to cover nearly $450 billion due by end-2030
Whether its first-half loss means it spent $80.7 billion of cash
check.why: Cash already covers the first year's $70 billion. The later bills are far bigger than its cash, so revenue has to pay them.

takeaways: Long contracts are future bills: test near bills against cash, later bills against revenue.
Anthropic promised about $895 billion for computing, seven times its cash, betting revenue keeps surging.
Watch for Anthropic's IPO price range and share count, which are not yet set.

sections.title: World
sections.gist: A Russian strike kills at least 24 after Ukraine's longest truce ends; the US drops South Africa and Rwanda from duty-free trade.

items.headline: Russian strike on Ukraine aid centre kills at least 24
items.text: On 2 November, Ukrainian authorities said a Russian air strike hit a humanitarian aid centre in southern Ukraine. At least 24 people were killed. The aid centre was in the Zaporizhzhia region. The strike came a day after a short humanitarian truce ended in Kherson, the region next door. That Kherson ceasefire lasted six days, the longest of the war, before fighting returned. Separately, President Zelensky said on 1 November that Ukraine will stop hitting Russia's oil refineries if the US provides missiles. It is not yet known whether the US will respond to that offer.
items.background: Ukraine and Russia are at war. A six-day humanitarian truce in Ukraine's Kherson region, the longest ceasefire of the war, had just ended.
items.why: The war's longest truce ended and a deadly strike followed within a day. Zelensky's offer links Ukraine's refinery strikes to US missile supplies.

items.headline: US drops South Africa and Rwanda from duty-free trade scheme
items.text: On 2 November the US said it will suspend South Africa and Rwanda from AGOA, its duty-free trade scheme for sub-Saharan Africa. The suspension starts on 1 January 2027. Duty-free means goods enter the US without import taxes. South Africa exported about $1.7bn of goods to the US under AGOA in 2025, including cars and farm products. Those exports will now face US import taxes. The Trump administration says both countries are breaking AGOA's rules. US Trade Representative Jamieson Greer cited practices that do not fit the scheme's eligibility criteria. Watch for responses from South Africa and Rwanda before 1 January 2027.
items.background: AGOA is a US programme that lets eligible sub-Saharan African countries sell many goods to the US without import taxes.
items.why: There is no direct effect on India. It shows the US removing trade benefits from countries it says break its rules.

sections.title: India
sections.gist: Opposition rally demands the election chief resign as Amit Shah defends SIR; Goyal says the US trade deal protects farmers.

items.headline: Amit Shah defends voter-roll revision after opposition rally in Delhi
items.text: On 1 November, tens of thousands of people joined an opposition march to Delhi's Ramlila Maidan, led by Rahul Gandhi. The protesters demanded that India's election chief resign over the voter-list overhaul, known as SIR. On 2 November, Union Home Minister Amit Shah defended SIR at an event in Hyderabad. He mocked the opposition's 'mock Parliament', a staged protest session. He also offered a special session of Parliament to debate SIR. It is not yet known whether the opposition will accept the offer, or when such a session might be held.
items.background: SIR is a revision of India's voter lists. Opposition parties object to it and want India's election chief to resign over it.
items.why: Voter lists decide who can vote in India. The dispute is now a direct fight between the government and the opposition.

items.headline: Goyal says India–US trade deal will fully protect farmers
items.text: On 29 October Commerce Minister Piyush Goyal said the interim India–US trade deal is in its final stages. He said it will fully protect Indian farmers. Goyal said no sensitive interest of farmers or others will be compromised once details are released. Under the deal, India will remove or cut import taxes on some US farm goods. These include tree nuts, fruit and DDGS, a leftover from ethanol-making used as animal feed. The deal builds on a February framework. That framework cut US import taxes on Indian goods from 50% to 18%, about a third of the earlier level. The text is still being fine-tuned. No signing date has been announced.
items.background: India and the US agreed a trade framework in February. They are now finishing an interim deal on tariffs, which are import taxes.
items.why: Lower US tariffs help Indian exporters. Cheaper US farm imports could affect what Indian farmers earn.

sections.title: Your money & life
sections.gist: Char Dham helicopter operators stopped pilgrim flights from Dehradun on 2 November to protest a new co-pilot rule brought in after a fatal crash.

items.headline: Char Dham helicopter operators stop pilgrim flights over co-pilot rule
items.text: On 2 November, helicopter operators stopped charter flights for Char Dham pilgrims from Dehradun. They are protesting a new rule from UCADA, the state aviation body, that makes a co-pilot mandatory on every flight. UCADA brought in the rule after a helicopter crash at Joshimath on 30 October killed six people. Operators say they cannot accept the rule "in its present form". They say paying for a second pilot would make flying "financially unviable". Helicopters are still bringing pilgrims who are already up there back down. A UCADA official said operators, UCADA and the DGCA, India's aviation regulator, were meeting to decide what happens next. The result of that meeting is not yet known.
items.background: Many Char Dham pilgrims take short charter helicopter flights from Dehradun to reach the hill shrines instead of making long road or foot journeys.
items.why: If you planned a Char Dham helicopter trip, new outbound flights from Dehradun are stopped. Return flights for pilgrims already there continue.

sections.title: Markets & money
sections.gist: On 2 November, Indian shares rose nearly 2% on Reliance and SEBI's tax proposal. Oil, gold and bond yields fell, and Meta weighed $20 billion in bonds.

items.headline: Reliance surges 11.6% as Indian markets jump nearly 2%
items.text: On 2 November, India's benchmark stock indices, the Nifty and Sensex, rose nearly 2%. Two things drove the buying. First, Reliance Industries shares jumped 11.6%, their best day since 2020. Second, SEBI, India's market regulator, has proposed rolling back the long-term capital gains (LTCG) tax. LTCG tax is the tax on profit from investments held for a long time. Lower tax on those gains can make holding shares more attractive. It is not yet known whether the government will accept SEBI's proposal.
items.background: SEBI regulates India's stock markets. It has proposed rolling back the tax on long-term investment profits, which the government would decide on.
items.why: Many Indians hold shares and mutual funds. A change in LTCG tax would change how much they keep from their gains.

items.headline: Oil falls most since July as Goldman raises Brent forecast
items.text: On 2 November, oil prices fell in their biggest one-day drop since July. The fall came on hopes for more talks with Iran. On the same day, Goldman Sachs raised its December forecast for Brent crude, the main global oil price, to $105 a barrel. US Treasury and European bond yields also fell as oil dropped. A bond yield is the return investors earn for lending to a government. Gold, meanwhile, opened on 2 November at its lowest level in over a year, ahead of the US midterm elections.
items.background: Brent crude is the benchmark price for much of the world's oil. Gold and government bonds are where many investors park money.
items.why: Oil and gold both made unusual moves on 2 November: oil's biggest fall since July, gold's lowest open in over a year.

items.headline: Meta reportedly weighing at least $20 billion in bond sales
items.text: On 2 November, Bloomberg News reported that Meta is weighing bond offerings worth at least $20 billion. A bond is a loan from investors that a company repays with interest. The potential sale would be cross-border, meaning sold to investors in more than one country. The money would fund Meta's AI infrastructure. It follows Meta's planned $97.5 billion equity fundraising, which means raising money by selling shares. The bond amount would be about one-fifth the size of that share sale. Timing and final size have not been reported.
items.background: Big tech companies are spending heavily on AI infrastructure. Meta already plans a $97.5 billion share sale to raise money.
items.why: Meta may borrow at least $20 billion on top of a $97.5 billion share sale, showing the scale of AI spending.

sections.title: Tech & AI
sections.gist: Courts are testing social media's harm to children: Snap settled a US addiction case, and Reddit challenged Australia's under-16 ban.

items.headline: Snap settles teen social media harm case in Los Angeles
items.text: On 2 November, Snap, the company behind Snapchat, settled with two teenagers in a Los Angeles case. The case tested claims that social media caused depression and eating disorders. The terms were not disclosed. Reuters described the deal as reached during the trial. Bloomberg gave more detail: the deal came partway through jury selection, the first stage of a trial, when jurors are chosen. By settling, Snap avoided going through the next high-profile social media addiction trial. It is not yet known how the settlement affects other similar cases.
items.background: Families in the US are suing social media companies, claiming their apps harmed young users' mental health.
items.why: The case tested whether social media firms can be held responsible for harm to teenagers, an issue for app users everywhere.

items.headline: Reddit challenges Australia's under-16 social media ban in High Court
items.text: Australia's ban on social media for under-16s faced its first major court challenge on 3 November. Two groups brought the case to the High Court, Australia's top court. They are Reddit and the Digital Freedom Project, a group led by New South Wales state MP John Ruddick. They argue the ban breaks the "implied freedom of political communication". That is a protection Australian courts have read into the constitution, even though it is not written there in words. The BBC says the rights group will argue the ban takes away under-16s' right to communicate freely. The date of the court's decision is not yet known.
items.background: Australia's ban, described by the BBC as world-leading, stops under-16s from holding social media accounts. Other countries are watching how it works.
items.why: Several countries are weighing similar age limits for social media. This case tests whether such a ban can survive a legal challenge.

sections.title: Science, health & climate
sections.gist: A bird flu death in Washington state is linked to dairy cattle, and NASA's Swift telescope should fall to Earth around 4 November.

items.headline: Yakima County resident dies of bird flu caught from dairy cattle
items.text: A Yakima County resident who was in hospital with severe avian influenza (bird flu) has died, the Yakima Health District reported on 2 November. The person had underlying health conditions. They caught the virus after contact with infected cattle at a dairy in the county. The district also confirmed a third human case in the county. That person was also exposed to dairy cattle and has not been seriously ill or in hospital. As of 29 October, H5N1 bird flu had been found in 33 dairy herds in Yakima County and one in Benton County, according to the state agriculture department. Officials say the risk to the general public remains low.
items.background: H5N1 is a bird flu virus that has spread into US dairy cattle. People mostly catch it through close contact with infected animals.
items.why: Officials say dairy workers and people with close or long contact with infected animals face the most risk, not the general public.

items.headline: NASA's Swift telescope set to fall to Earth around 4 November
items.text: NASA's Swift space telescope is expected to fall back to Earth after a rescue mission failed. The US Space Force's latest prediction, reported by Popular Science on 2 November, has Swift re-entering the atmosphere on or around Wednesday, 4 November. The 2,500-pound observatory will mostly burn up on the way down. Swift's record is large. It studied more than 2,000 gamma-ray bursts and more than 1,400 supernovae (exploding stars). It also recorded stars being torn apart by black holes and helped document the interstellar comet 3I/ATLAS. About 7,000 scientific papers use its data. Watch for the final re-entry time once the Space Force confirms it.
items.background: Swift is a NASA space telescope that catches gamma-ray bursts, the brightest explosions in the universe, and quickly turns to study them.
items.why: Astronomers worldwide lose a key tool for fast-changing events in the sky; about 7,000 papers have relied on its data.

sections.title: Cricket — the masala
sections.gist: Glenn Maxwell quits international cricket, the IPL retention deadline moves to 17 November, Pant faces a fitness test, and Tilak Varma leads India A.

items.headline: Glenn Maxwell, 38, quits international cricket but stays in BBL
items.text: Australia's Glenn Maxwell, 38, has retired from international cricket, including T20 internationals, ESPNcricinfo and The Guardian reported on 2 November. He has also ended his first-class and List A career. That means no more red-ball matches and no more official 50-over games for him. But he is not leaving the game fully. Maxwell remains available to play for Melbourne Stars in the Big Bash League (BBL), Australia's T20 club league. The Guardian marked his exit with the nickname fans gave him: 'Big Show'. His next matches, if any, will come in Stars colours.
items.background: First-class cricket means multi-day red-ball matches; List A means official 50-over matches. The BBL is Australia's city-based T20 league.
items.why: Indian fans lose a familiar opponent from Australia's T20 side, though he can still play in franchise cricket.

items.headline: IPL retention deadline moved to 17 November for India-NZ ODIs
items.text: The BCCI has moved the IPL player retention deadline back by two days, to 17 November, The Hindu and Outlook India reported on 2 November. Retention is when each team names the players it will keep; the rest go into the auction. The change is understood to be because of the India-New Zealand ODI series. Its fifth and final match is on 15 November. The date of the mini-auction stays the same. Teams now have until 17 November to send in their lists.
items.background: Before each IPL auction, teams must submit lists of players they keep. Everyone released can then be bought by any team.
items.why: The lists show which stars stay with your IPL team and who goes into the auction pool.

items.headline: Pant faces fitness test; Tilak Varma to lead India A
items.text: Rishabh Pant will take a fitness test before India leave for New Zealand, ESPNcricinfo reported on 2 November. He hurt his side (a side strain, a muscle injury along the ribs) during the Irani Cup. He has been at the BCCI Centre of Excellence in Bengaluru since 23 October. Separately, Tilak Varma will captain a 15-member India A squad at the ACC Men's Rising Stars Asia Cup. This 50-over event runs in Doha, Qatar, from 19 to 29 November. Rajat Patidar is vice-captain. The squad includes Harshit Rana, Abhishek Sharma and Vaibhav Sooryavanshi.
items.background: India A is the second-string national team, used to test players close to the senior side. The BCCI Centre of Excellence treats injured players.
items.why: Pant's test decides if he joins the New Zealand tour; the India A squad shows who selectors are watching.

quiz.q: Brent fell over 3% on 2 November. What best explains the fall?
options: A ceasefire deal was signed that day
A report made more diplomacy before any strikes look likelier
Hormuz fully reopened to tankers
quiz.why: No deal was signed and Hormuz did not reopen. A report that Trump wants more time for talks changed the odds, and the price followed.

quiz.q: A candidate leads by 2,000 votes and only 1,500 ballots are left. Can the race be called?
options: No, every race must wait for a full count
Yes, because even winning every remaining ballot, the trailer cannot catch up
Only if the remaining ballots are mail ballots
quiz.why: The trailer can gain at most 1,500 votes. That is less than the 2,000-vote gap, so the result cannot change.

quiz.q: Why would a community care which district's police chief covers its village?
options: That chief's officers lead the investigation, gather evidence and make arrests.
That chief decides the punishment for anyone found guilty.
That chief controls the state's elected government.
quiz.why: Police build the case by collecting evidence and making arrests. Courts decide punishment. So if people distrust the investigator, they doubt the whole case.
